Essential revisions:

A number of concerns were raised by the reviewers that preclude acceptance at this stage. The paper could be substantially improved without new experiments but requiring new analysis and rewriting. The story may change quite a bit and may end up having much less to do with differences in the developmental timelines between zebrin regions, and much more to do with differences in the developmental timelines between lobules. The link between stripes compartmentalization and Purkinje cells maturation is weak since the authors choose to characterize lobules far apart in the antero-posterior axis. The paper will be no less interesting by focusing on specific lobules without mentioning their zebrin identity that can be discussed in the end. The question of when PCs reach maturity in the specific lobules is important and will clearly enhance the quality of the paper. The authors should be able to provide the exact PCs localization together with specific features in the different lobules. By reorganizing the data, they might be in position to compare lobule I, II or III together with IX and X…

The consensus of the reviewers is that the authors should address:

1. The properties of Purkinje cells in lobules involved in eyeblink conditioning reach maturity later than in lobules involved in VOR adaptation. Showing this will require new analyses since as it stands, none of the figures really show when the properties of Purkinje cells reach maturity in any lobules.

2. Eyeblink conditioning is impaired in juvenile mice at the time when the properties of Purkinje cells in the eyeblink lobules have yet to reach maturity, whereas VOR adaptation is fine at that same time. Again, showing this will also require new analyses since the current evaluation of VOR adaptation is insufficient to know whether the juvenile mice are impaired or not.

Showing 1 and 2 would provide useful information for the field, even if the results are correlational. In general, we know very little about the developmental timeline of Purkinje cell properties in different regions of the cerebellum, and the paper would speak to that. It would have been useful to look at the developmental timeline of plasticity in Purkinje cells of different lobules, but that will require new experiments and is beyond the scope of revision.

If in addition to 1 and 2, the authors were able to convincingly show that the properties of Purkinje cells in other zebrin- regions (in addition to the eyeblink regions) reach maturity late, while those in other zebrin+ regions (in addition to the VOR regions) reach maturity early, then the paper would be stronger. But showing whether their findings apply to zebrin- and zebrin+ regions, IN GENERAL, may not be possible.

Detailed comments of the reviews support these concerns and provide further guidance.

Reviewer #1:

In their manuscript "Differential spatio-temporal development of Purkinje cell subsets shapes the emergence of cerebellum-dependent behaviors ", Beekholf et al., combined several in vitro and state-of-the art in vivo approaches to characterize the developmental trajectories of distinct Purkinje cells (PCs) localized in Zebrin + or Zebrin – region of the cerebellum. They found that several intrinsic features of PCs development are differentially regulated in a zebrin II-dependent manner. The timing of PCs maturation in these regions (Zebrin+ or Zebrin -) is mirrored by specific cerebellum-dependent behavioral acquisition. Overall, I found the study to be very straight-forward and the presented data are fairly supportive of their conclusion, although mainly correlative.

I only have a few concerns:

1. The overall heterogeneity of PCs intrinsic activities within the same lobule can be clearly observed in Figure 1 and Figure 2. For example, some plots distribution (in Fig1C1, C2 or Supp 1B1, 1B2) appeared bimodal. A population with high SS activity (SS rate above 60hz) and one with low SS activity (SS rate Below 35hz) at P12-P17 can clearly be observed. Since the authors labelled the recording sites with biocytin, it will be interesting to relate the PCs location to PCs intrinsic activities.

2. One important statement of the manuscript is that early developmental trajectory of PCs is zebrinII-dependent. However, in early and late phase of cerebellar development, the strict identification of ZebrinII+ domain is challenging. It is not certain whether early PCs identified as Zebrin II+ are related to each of the PC ZebrinII + stripes in the adult. Although the idea is attractive and the correlative data in lobule III and X showed distinct PC features, one might argue that change in PC molecular identity during development within a specific lobule is likely. The author should discussed this possibility or add new arguments to strengthen their hypothesis.

3. PC morphology can vary depending on their location within the same lobule. One localized at the base or at the apex of the cerebellar cortex follium have significant different morphological features (A. Sudarov and A. L. Joyner 2007). The authors should indicate where the PCs were quantified and provide their overall localization within a lobule.

4. A clear identification of PC molecular signature during development is not trivial unless longitudinal clonal study can be performed in PCs. Is it possible to dismiss the existence of an anteroposterior developmental gradient of PC maturation? For example, did PCs present is lobule I showed distinct intrinsic activities from those in lobule III, both being Zebrin II+.

Reviewer #2:

This manuscript by Beekhof et al. examines the morphological and physiological development of zebrin + and zebrin – Purkinje cells in the cerebellum and relate this to emergence of cerebellum dependent behaviors in each region. The authors examined simple spike firing rate and regularity, complex spike rate and regularity, dendritic morphology, density of climbing fiber synapses, and axonal arborization of zebrin +/- Purkinje cells across a range of ages (P3- adult). They find that zebrin + and – Purkinje cells differ across many of these measurements (as has been observed previously), but critically, they find that zebrin – Purkinje cells typically reach mature phenotypes at younger ages compared to zebrin + Purkinje cells. From these results, the authors hypothesize that zebrin – circuits may mature more quickly. They test this by training young and old mice in VOR phase reversal (a behavior largely dependent on zebrin – circuits) and delay eyeblink conditioning (a behavior largely dependent on zebrin + circuits). Indeed, they find that young mice exhibit robust VOR learning but impaired eyeblink conditioning, consistent with earlier maturation of Zebrin – Purkinje cells.

In general, I find the data regarding the development of zebrin +/- Purkinje cells to be thorough and convincing. I am more concerned about the behavioral data and whether the behavioral differences can really be attributed to the differences observed in the first half of the paper.

My major concerns related to the use and interpretation of the behavioral experiments.

1. The authors want to draw a connection between the behavioral results and the development of zebrin +/- Purkinje cells. In my opinion, this is a tenuous connection supported by little evidence. There is a somewhat weak correlation between behavior and the measured properties of Purkinje cells, but little or nothing to suggest causation here. There are any number of other factors that could result in delayed learning of eyeblink conditioning compared to VOR adaptation. Some of these are considered in the discussion, but the link between development of zebrin +/- Purkinje cells and behavioral outcomes should be toned down.

2. Learning during VOR adaptation or eyeblink conditioning likely engages Purkinje cell plasticity (either in the form of parallel fiber LTP/LTD or changes in intrinsic excitability), yet these parameters were not examined across age or zebrin region, why not?

3. My final concern regarding the behavior experiments is with the underlying assumption that behavioral learning always improves with cellular/circuit development. The finding that VOR adaptation is more efficient in juvenile animals (compared to adults) contradicts this assumption. I don't think you can say that because VOR adaptation is faster in juveniles, that the underlying circuits have developed earlier compared to the circuits underlying eyeblink conditioning. It could be argued that the VOR circuits are in fact in an immature hyperplastic state in juvenile mice, and this is not evidence of more fully developed Purkinje cells.

Reviewer #3:

This work is a follow-up to the authors' previous study demonstrating that the properties of Purkinje cells in zebrin+ and zebrin- compartments differ in multiple ways. Now, they have shown when these differences emerge during development, and tested whether these timelines correlate with the emergence of zebrin+ and zebrin- dependent behaviors. The experiments are technically impressive, including longitudinal evaluation of electrophysiologal properties (in vivo and in vitro) and morphology of Purkinje cells, as well as analysis of cerebellum-dependent behaviors in juvenile mice directly after weaning. The results are important because they provide a first glimpse into the developmental timelines of Purkinje cells in two separate regions of the cerebellum (anterior cerebellum and nodulus), and the impact that ontogenetic differences in these timelines may have in early motor function.

There are a number of concerns that need to be addressed. With the exception of concern 4, however, none of these concerns require new experiments and could be adequately addressed with new analysis and text revisions.

1. One of the main claims is that the properties of Purkinje cells in zebrin+ compartments reach mature levels earlier than in zebrin- compartments. However, most of the analysis and all of the figures are focused on comparing when the differences between Purkinje cells in zebrin+ and zebrin- emerge during development. This is a different question. The analysis and the figures should be redone to assess when the properties of Purkinje cells reach maturity, rather than assessing when the properties of zebrin+ and zebrin- Purkinje cells become different from each other. It will be critical to specify the criterion used to determine whether Purkinje cell properties have reached maturity. For example, Figure 4B2 shows many more VGluT2 puncta in zebrin+ than in zebrin- Purkinje cells by age P7, but it would be wrong to assume that this means that VGluT2 expression has reached maturity in zebrin+ compartments by age P7 because the number of VGluT2 puncta undergoes extensive remodeling after that age and is dramatically reduced on P14 and P21, before starting to go up again at P35.

2. Another claim is that VOR learning is actually enhanced in juvenile mice relative to adult mice. However, the data shown is not sufficient. A more complete analysis is necessary, including: (1) a full evaluation of the eye movements of the juvenile and adult mice during the training period. Previous work has shown that the best predictor of VOR learning in mice is related to the gaze signals present during training (Shin et al., J Neurosci., 2014), and it is important to rule out differences in gaze as the root cause of the learning differences, (2) a complete evaluation of the eye movements of the juvenile and adult mice during the test periods. Currently, the analysis is restricted to assessing the phase of the learned eye movements (Figure 6A2), and there's no information about their gain, (3) To formally test whether learning is enhanced, it will be necessary to perform an analysis to determine whether the learned movements (not just the phase of those movements) are more adaptive in juvenile or adult mice. It would be interesting if it turned out that the learned movements of juvenile and adult mice achieve similar performance levels, but using different adaptive mechanisms.

3. Throughout the paper, the terms "zebrin-" and "zebrin+" are used interchangeably with the terms "anterior cerebellum" and "nodular cerebellum". In reality, however, the majority of the experiments were performed by comparing the properties of Purkinje cells in one region of the anterior cerebellum (lobules I-III) and one specific region in the nodular cerebellum (lobules IX-X). While it is true that most Purkinje cells in lobule I-III are zebrin- and most Purkinje cells in lobule IX-X are zebrin+, it unclear whether the developmental timeline of Purkinje cells in lobule I-III (or IX-X) will apply to all other zebrin+ (or zebrin-) regions of the cerebellum. For this reason, it is critical to specify the lobular location for each one of the analyses performed. It looks like all the experiments in Figure 2 were performed in only lobule III and lobule X, while experiments in Figure 3 and 4 were performed in lobules I-III and IX-X, but it is unclear whether most of the Purkinje cells were located in one of the specific lobules. In addition, there is no information about the location of the Purkinje cells in Figure 1 and Figure 5, or whether most of the Purkinje cells in these figures came from specific lobules. Unless zebrin+ and zebrin- Purkinje cells were sampled in enough numbers from all lobules, it is not possible to make general claims. For instance, if the results show that Purkinje cells in lobule III (which are zebrin-) reach maturity early on, it is incorrect to assume that zebrin- Purkinje cells in other lobules of the cerebellar cortex will also reach maturity early on. For analyses done by measuring the properties of Purkinje cells in specific lobules, the text of the paper should be revised by replacing all claims about the properties of Purkinje cells in zebrin+ and zebrin- compartments (including in the Figures) with claims about the properties of Purkinje cells in those specific lobules.

4. The regions of the cerebellar cortex involved in the two behaviors that were examined are the flocculus (for VOR adaptation) and lobules IV-V-VI (for eyeblink conditioning). The paper should report the properties and developmental timelines of Purkinje cells located in those specific lobules since it cannot be assumed that the properties and developmental timelines of Purkinje cells in lobules I-III will be the same as in IV-V-VI, or that the properties and developmental timelines of Purkinje cells in lobules IX-X will be the same as in the flocculus.

claims.claim: PC firing rate significantly increases from P3-P5 to P10-P11 in both lobule III and lobule X.
claims.source: PC firing rate significantly increases from P3-P5 to P10-P11 (LIII p=0.0002; LX p=0.0007), but over these first days of development there were no differences in the firing rate between PCs of different cerebellar regions (Figure 2A2,B1-Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claims.claim: Over the first days of development (P3-P5 to P10-P11) there were no differences in the firing rate between PCs of different cerebellar regions.
claims.source: PC firing rate significantly increases from P3-P5 to P10-P11 (LIII p=0.0002; LX p=0.0007), but over these first days of development there were no differences in the firing rate between PCs of different cerebellar regions (Figure 2A2,B1-Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claims.claim: Starting from P12 to P17, the intrinsic activity of PCs located in lobule X is significantly different from those located in lobule III.
claims.source: Starting from P12 to P17, similar to the in vivo data, we observed that the intrinsic activity of PCs located in lobule X is significantly different from those located in lobule III (LIII: 51.7 ± 3.4 Hz; LX: 34.8 ± 2.0 Hz, p=0.008, Figure 2B1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claims.claim: After P12-P17, the differences in intrinsic firing rate in PCs from both cerebellar regions are maintained into adulthood.
claims.source: After this key point during development, the differences in intrinsic firing rate in PCs from both cerebellar regions are maintained into adulthood (>P60, LIII: 61.2 ± 2.5 Hz; LX: 46.3 ± 1.9 Hz, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claims.claim: There is a significant increase in irregularity in lobule III PCs from P18 when compared with lobule X PCs.
claims.source: In line with the in vivo results (Figure 1B2), there is a significant increase in irregularity in lobule III PCs from P18 when compared with lobule X PCs (CV2, LIII: 0.11 ± 0.01; LX: 0.05 ± 0.00, p<0.0001) and this is maintained into adulthood (>P60, CV2, LIII: 0.11 ± 0.01; LX: 0.04 ± 0.00, p<0.0001) (Figure 2B2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claims.claim: Differences in SS firing rate at least in lobules III and X are indeed the result of differences of intrinsic activity of distinct PC subpopulations starting at P12-P17 and maintained into mature ages.
claims.source: All together, these data indicate that differences in SS firing rate at least in lobules III and X are indeed the result of differences of intrinsic activity of distinct PC subpopulations starting at P12-P17 and maintained into mature ages.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro recording data.

claims.claim: From P6-P11 to P12-17 there is a rapid increase in dendritic complexity and area across all PCs.
claims.source: Concomitantly with the physiology data, we observed that from P6-P11 to P12-17 there is a rapid increase in dendritic complexity and area (Figure 3A) across all PCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference in dendritic complexity, maximum length, and area between PCs in anterior (lobules I/II/III) and nodular (lobules IX/X) regions at P12-P17.
claims.source: However, unlike in the physiological data there is no significant difference in dendritic complexity (P12-P17, LI-III: 336.1 ± 31.7; LIX-X: 291.2 ± 17.1, p=0.38, Figure 3B1), maximum length (P12-P17, LI-III: 138.3 ± 5.1 µm; LIX-X: 142.5 ± 3.9 µm, p=0.74, Figure 3B2), and area (P12-P17, LI-III: 5419 ± 399 µm2; LI-X: 6109 ± 462 µm2, p=0.46, Figure 3B3) between PCs in anterior (lobules I/II/III) and nodular (lobules IX/X) regions at P12-P17.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claims.claim: Dendritic arborization in lobules IX-X marginally changed after P12-P17.
claims.source: While dendritic arborization in lobules IX-X marginally changed after this time point, dendritic complexity significantly increased in lobules I-III from the third postnatal week (from P18) into adulthood: dendritic complexity (P60, LI-III: 663.1 ± 23.8; LIX-X: 445.7 ± 22.2, p<0.0001, Figure 3B1), maximum length (P60, LI-III: 206.6 ± 5.9 µm; LIX-X: 169.9 ± 4.0 µm, p<0.0001, Figure 3B2), and area (P60, LI-III: 10890 ± 412 µm2; LIX-X: 8520 ± 377 µm2, p<0.0001, Figure 3B3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claims.claim: Dendritic complexity significantly increased in lobules I-III from the third postnatal week (from P18) into adulthood.
claims.source: While dendritic arborization in lobules IX-X marginally changed after this time point, dendritic complexity significantly increased in lobules I-III from the third postnatal week (from P18) into adulthood: dendritic complexity (P60, LI-III: 663.1 ± 23.8; LIX-X: 445.7 ± 22.2, p<0.0001, Figure 3B1), maximum length (P60, LI-III: 206.6 ± 5.9 µm; LIX-X: 169.9 ± 4.0 µm, p<0.0001, Figure 3B2), and area (P60, LI-III: 10890 ± 412 µm2; LIX-X: 8520 ± 377 µm2, p<0.0001, Figure 3B3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claims.claim: A difference in size and complexity in dendritic arborization of PC subpopulations can be first observed at P18.
claims.source: A difference in size and complexity in dendritic arborization of PC subpopulations can therefore be first observed at P18 (see Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claims.claim: At P7 there was a significant increase in VGluT2 puncta in lobules IX-X when compared with lobules I-III.
claims.source: Remarkably, we found that at P7 there was a significant increase in VGluT2 puncta in lobules IX-X (P7, LI-III: 0.62 ± 0.31%; LIX-X: 3.87 ± 0.19%, p<0.0001, Figure 4B2) when compared with lobules I-III.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: At P7 the percentage of CF extension into the molecular layer was significantly increased in lobules IX-X compared to lobules I-III.
claims.source: As a result, at P7 the percentage of CF extension into the molecular layer (ML) was significantly increased in lobules IX-X (P7, LI-III: 11.1 ± 1.1%; LIX-X: 80.5 ± 1.0%, p<0.0001, Figure 4B3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: CF translocation starts earlier in nodular lobules.
claims.source: These results suggest that CF translocation starts earlier in nodular lobules (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunohistochemical data on VGluT2 puncta and CF extension.

claims.claim: From P7 to P14, there was a dramatic increase in ML thickness in both regions of the cerebellum.
claims.source: From P7 to P14, there was a dramatic increase in ML thickness in both regions of the cerebellum (Figure 4B1) but the significant difference in VGluT2 puncta and CF terminals disappeared (VGluT2 puncta, P7: p<0.0001, P14: p=0.78; CF terminals, P7: p<0.0001, P14: p=0.24, Figure 4B2 and B3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: From P21 into adulthood, there was a significant increase in ML thickness in lobules I-III when compared with the nodular lobules.
claims.source: From P21 into adulthood, there was a significant increase in ML thickness in lobules I-III when compared with the nodular lobules (P60, LI-III: 137.5 ± 1.3 µm; Lob IX-X: 116.9 ± 4.9 µm, p<0.001, Figure 4B1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: CF translocation into the PC dendrite starts earlier in nodular lobules when compared with anterior lobules I, II, and III.
claims.source: These results indicate that CF translocation into the PC dendrite starts earlier in nodular lobules when compared with anterior lobules I, II, and III pointing to another difference in the maturation of the cerebellar circuitries in different cerebellar regions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunohistochemical data on CF development.

claims.claim: PC axons are present in the cerebellar nuclei as early as embryonic day (E) 15.5 in mice.
claims.source: PC axons are present in the cerebellar nuclei as early as embryonic day (E) 15.5 in mice (Sillitoe et al., 2009) and E18 in rats (Eisenman et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Targeting to the correct cerebellar subnuclei is already in place at very early points in cerebellar development.
claims.source: Targeting to the correct cerebellar subnuclei is also already in place at very early points in cerebellar development (Sillitoe et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: PC axons exhibit a multi-step developmental process in culture.
claims.source: In culture, PC axons exhibit a multi-step developmental process (de Luca et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: There are significant differences across age of PC axon arbor maximum length and complexity, as both parameters increase from P7 to P14 and then decrease at P21.
claims.source: This analysis revealed significant differences across age of PC axon arbor maximum length and complexity, as both parameters increase from P7 to P14 and then decrease at P21 (number of intersections, P7: 84.2 ± 18.2; P10: 254.4 ± 40.5; P14: 277.4 ± 17.5; P21: 296.4 ± 37.9, p=0.013; length, P7: 124.2 ± 17.8 µm; P10: 212.7 ± 24.4 µm; P14: 216.4 ± 14.3 µm2; P21: 225.2 ± 16.1 µm2, p=0.060, Figure 5C,E1, E2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claims.claim: Area taken up by the axon arbors continued to increase with age.
claims.source: Area taken up by the axon arbors, however, continued to increase with age (area, P7: 1.52 ± 0.20 µm2·103 P10: 1.47 ± 0.25 µm2·103; P14: 2.26 ± 0.19 µm2·103; P21: 3.07 ± 0.29 µm2·103, p<0.0001; Figure 5E3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claims.claim: Sholl analysis revealed significant differences between Z– and Z+ axon arbors at P10, P14 and P21, with Z– axon arbors exhibiting a denser branching complexity than Z+.
claims.source: Sholl analysis revealed significant differences between Z– and Z+ axon arbors at P10, P14 and P21, with Z– axon arbors exhibiting a denser branching complexity than Z+ (P10: p=0.0457; P14: p=0.0017; P21: p=0.0388).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claims.claim: Significant differences were found between Z– and Z+ groups for length and area but not number of intersections.
claims.source: Significant differences were found between Z– and Z+ groups for length and area but not number of intersections (intersections, p=0.252; length, p=0.0197; area, p=0.0257; Figure 5F1-3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claims.claim: PC axons reach near mature shapes already early in development, with a peak in size around P14 and subtle differences between Z– and Z+ axons.
claims.source: Taken together, our novel approach to analyze axon terminal development in cerebellar nuclei indicates that PC axons reach near mature shapes already early in development, with a peak in size around P14 and subtle differences between Z– and Z+ axons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morphological data on axon arbor development.

claims.claim: The VOR ensures the stabilization of images on the retina via compensatory eye movement every time the vestibular system is activated.
claims.source: The VOR ensures the stabilization of images on the retina via compensatory eye movement every time the vestibular system is activated (head movement).
claims.evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge about the VOR.

claims.claim: VOR adaptation is the adjustment of compensatory eye movements based on a mismatch between vestibular and visual input.
claims.source: VOR adaptation is the adjustment of compensatory eye movements based on a mismatch between vestibular and visual input, moving in the same or opposite direction (i.e. in or out of phase) (Ito, 1982; Nagao, 1989; Schonewille et al., 2010; Wulff et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Compensatory eye movements are controlled by the flocculus, together with the nodulus forming the vestibulocerebellum, which is predominantly Z+.
claims.source: Moreover, compensatory eye movements are controlled by the flocculus, together with the nodulus forming the vestibulocerebellum, which is predominantly Z+ (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Hawkes and Herrup, 1995; Sillitoe and Hawkes, 2002; Figure 6A1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: In the EBC paradigm, a neutral sensory stimulus alone leads to a well-timed eyeblink after repeated pairing with a noxious stimulus which induces a reflexive eyelid closure.
claims.source: In the EBC paradigm, a neutral sensory stimulus alone leads to a well-timed eyeblink after repeated pairing with a noxious stimulus which induces a reflexive eyelid closure (usually a mild airpuff) (Boele et al., 2010; McCormick and Thompson, 1984; Thompson and Steinmetz, 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The cerebellar eyeblink regions putatively reside in the anterior cerebellum, in particular at the border of lobule IV-V to VI, and from the hemisphere lobule IV-V to simplex, a region that is largely ZebrinII-negative.
claims.source: The cerebellar eyeblink regions putatively reside in the anterior cerebellum, in particular at the border of lobule IV-V to VI, and from the hemisphere lobule IV-V to simplex, a region that is largely ZebrinII-negative (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Hawkes and Herrup, 1995; Sillitoe and Hawkes, 2002; Heiney et al., 2014; Figure 6B1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Neither the OKR gain or phase differ significantly between juvenile and adult age groups.
claims.source: Neither the OKR gain or phase differ significantly between age groups (OKR gain, young: 0.60 ± 0.09; adult: 0.59 ± 0.10, p=0.84; and OKR phase, young: −15.5 ± 6.7; adult: −15.4 ± 5.0, p=0.96, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A1,B1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from compensatory eye movement recordings.

claims.claim: The VOR gain is significantly increased in adult mice when compared with juveniles.
claims.source: In contrast, the VOR gain is significantly increased (VOR gain, young: 0.42 ± 0.09; adult: 0.61 ± 0.09, p<0.0001, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A2) and the VOR phase decreased (VOR phase, young: 29.4 ± 5.8; adult: 21.4 ± 4.5, p=0.0024, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B2) in adult mice when compared with juveniles.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from compensatory eye movement recordings.

claims.claim: The VOR phase is decreased in adult mice when compared with juveniles.
claims.source: In contrast, the VOR gain is significantly increased (VOR gain, young: 0.42 ± 0.09; adult: 0.61 ± 0.09, p<0.0001, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A2) and the VOR phase decreased (VOR phase, young: 29.4 ± 5.8; adult: 21.4 ± 4.5, p=0.0024, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B2) in adult mice when compared with juveniles.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from compensatory eye movement recordings.

claims.claim: There are no differences in the VVOR phase between juvenile and adult mice.
claims.source: Moreover, while there are no differences in the VVOR phase (VVOR phase, young: 1.33 ± 0.46; adult: 1.35 ± 0.13, p=0.97, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B3), there is a significant increase in the VVOR gain of juvenile animals compared with adults (VVOR gain, young: 0.89 ± 0.01; adult: 0.96 ± 0.01, p=0.009, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from compensatory eye movement recordings.

claims.claim: There is a significant increase in the VVOR gain of juvenile animals compared with adults.
claims.source: Moreover, while there are no differences in the VVOR phase (VVOR phase, young: 1.33 ± 0.46; adult: 1.35 ± 0.13, p=0.97, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B3), there is a significant increase in the VVOR gain of juvenile animals compared with adults (VVOR gain, young: 0.89 ± 0.01; adult: 0.96 ± 0.01, p=0.009, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from compensatory eye movement recordings.

claims.claim: The training resulted in juvenile animals reversing their VOR phase faster with significantly lower gain values on the first 3 days and higher phase values on all days.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we observed that the training resulted in juvenile animals reversing their VOR phase, probed in the dark with only vestibular stimulation, faster with significantly lower gain values on the first 3 days and higher phase values on all days (VOR gain, days 1–3, all p<0.01 phase reversal, all p<0.0001, Figure 6A2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from VOR phase reversal training.

claims.claim: Consolidation is significantly larger in juvenile mice than in adult mice, for gain decrease and for phase increase.
claims.source: Consolidation is significantly larger in juvenile mice than in adult mice, for gain decrease (p=0.0005) and for phase increase (p=0.0006 and p=0.0069, respectively, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from VOR phase reversal training.

claims.claim: Juvenile animals exhibit a significantly lower CR percentage after the first day of learning when compared with the adult animals.
claims.source: Juvenile animals exhibit a significantly lower CR percentage after the first day of learning (juvenile: 20.4 ± 4.4%; adult: 30.9 ± 6.0%, p=0.027, Figure 6B2) when compared with the adult animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from eyeblink conditioning.

claims.claim: The amplitude of the eyelid closure in response to the conditioned stimulus is reduced in juvenile animals.
claims.source: Moreover, the amplitude of the eyelid closure in response to the conditioned stimulus (fraction eyelid closure) is reduced in juvenile animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A2,C1,C2,C3,C4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from eyeblink conditioning.

claims.claim: The difference in CR percentage was not due to reduced eyelid closure abilities in juvenile mice because UR timing and onset is similar between the two groups.
claims.source: The difference in CR percentage was not due to reduced eyelid closure abilities in juvenile mice because UR timing and onset is similar between the two groups (UR onset, young: 5.61 ± 0.15; adult: 6.41 ± 0.10, p=0.41; UR peak time, young: 67.2 ± 1.0; adult: 69.0 ± 1.0, p=0.55, Figure 6—figure supplement 4A1,B1,B2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from eyeblink conditioning.

claims.claim: Juvenile animals had an attenuated rate of EBC acquisition while the VOR adaptation was heightened in juvenile animals when compared with adult animals.
claims.source: Taken together, our data indicate that juvenile animals had an attenuated rate of EBC acquisition while the VOR adaptation was heightened in juvenile animals when compared with adult animals.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Different developmental timelines in distinct cerebellar regions underlie the emergency of cerebellar specific behaviors.
claims.source: This suggests different developmental timelines in distinct cerebellar regions underlie the emergency of cerebellar specific behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integration of physiological, morphological, and behavioral data.

claims.claim: Different subpopulations of PCs acquire unique morphological and physiological features during distinct developmental timelines, such that PCs of the posterior cerebellum, particularly lobule X, reach their adult stage prior to PCs of the anterior, in e.g. lobule III, cerebellum.
claims.source: In this study, we uncover that different subpopulations of PCs acquire unique morphological and physiological features during distinct developmental timelines, such that PCs of the posterior cerebellum, particularly lobule X, reach their adult stage prior to PCs of the anterior, in e.g. lobule III, cerebellum (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claims.claim: Cerebellar compartmentalization has been shown to correlate with PCs birth dates: early-born (E10-E11.5) will become adult Z+ PCs and late-born (E11.5-E13) will become adult Z– PCs.
claims.source: Cerebellar compartmentalization has been shown to correlate with PCs birth dates: early-born (E10-E11.5) will become adult Z+ PCs and late-born (E11.5-E13) will become adult Z– PCs (Hashimoto and Mikoshiba, 2003; Namba et al., 2011; Larouche and Hawkes, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: There is a strong relationship between embryonic compartments and adult zonal patterning associated with the modular organization of the olivo-cortico-nuclear circuit.
claims.source: Thus, there is a strong relationship between embryonic compartments and adult zonal patterning associated with the modular organization of the olivo-cortico-nuclear circuit (Brochu et al., 1990; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007a; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Voogd et al., 2003; Pijpers and Ruigrok, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The maturation of the zonal phenotype is only complete around P12-P15, based on the molecular markers ZebrinII or PLCβ4.
claims.source: The maturation of the zonal phenotype is only complete around P12-P15, based on the molecular markers ZebrinII (Brochu et al., 1990; Lannoo et al., 1991) or PLCβ4 (76).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Lobule X/Z+ PCs reached adult stable properties earlier than anterior lobule III/Z– PCs, particularly when it comes to simple and complex spike activity, as well as dendritic morphology.
claims.source: In our studies, developmental electrophysiological and morphological analyses revealed that lobule X/Z+ PCs reached adult stable properties earlier than anterior lobule III/Z– PCs (Figure 7), particularly when it comes to simple and complex spike activity, as well as dendritic morphology.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claims.claim: The configuration of mature PCs follows directly from their development, which is a consequence of their birthdate.
claims.source: This suggests that the configuration of mature PCs follows directly from their development, which is a consequence of their birthdate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the developmental data and previous research on PC birthdates.

claims.claim: Signs of ZebrinII-related differentiation in the electrophysiological properties could already be detected in the end at the second postnatal week from P12.
claims.source: Signs of ZebrinII-related differentiation in the electrophysiological properties, similar to those observed in firing rate of SS in the adult mouse in vivo (Zhou et al., 2014), could already be detected in the end at the second postnatal week from P12 (Figure 1C1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claims.claim: Z+ PCs demonstrate early maturation of their physiological properties by reaching a SS activity level in vivo at P18 that is not significantly different from that in adulthood.
claims.source: Z+ PCs demonstrate early maturation of their physiological properties by reaching a SS activity level in vivo at P18 that is not significantly different from that in adulthood.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claims.claim: In PCs from anterior regions of the cerebellum the activity continues to gradually increase until adulthood.
claims.source: Contrarily, in PCs from anterior regions of the cerebellum the activity continues to gradually increase until adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claims.claim: CS activity also showed reduced activity of Z+ PCs compared with Z– PC CSs from P18-P27.
claims.source: Similarly, CS activity, which results exclusively from the activity of neurons in the inferior olive, also showed reduced activity of Z+ PCs compared with Z– PC CSs from P18-P27 (Figure 1D1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claims.claim: Physiological differences in two populations of PCs are first detected at the end of the second postnatal week and result from intrinsic differences combined with an input component.
claims.source: Overall, physiological differences in two populations of PCs are first detected at the end of the second postnatal week and result from intrinsic differences combined with an input component (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the physiological data.

claims.claim: Changes in physiological properties during development match the time course of dendritic growth in rats.
claims.source: Previous reports have shown that, in rats, changes in physiological properties during development match the time course of dendritic growth, without differentiating subtypes (McKay and Turner, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Starting from P18, PCs of the anterior lobule III continue to grow and develop a larger dendritic area and more elaborated dendritic tree when compared with the nodular lobule X PCs.
claims.source: Starting from P18, PCs of the anterior lobule III continue to grow and develop a larger dendritic area and more elaborated dendritic tree when compared with the nodular lobule X PCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claims.claim: PCs in the nodular lobule X region appear to reach their adult stage at P18, although a smaller growth is still present from the adolescent to adult stage.
claims.source: Similar to our physiology data, PCs in the nodular lobule X region appear to reach their adult stage at P18, although a smaller growth is still present from the adolescent to adult stage.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claims.claim: In some populations of PCs their maturation is not only linked with their location in the cerebellum, but also coupled to their physiological development.
claims.source: This suggests that in some populations of PCs their maturation is not only linked with their location in the cerebellum (Altman, 1972), but also coupled to their physiological development.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between physiological and morphological development.

claims.claim: Mossy fiber and CF afferents terminate into parasagittal domains that align with the ZebrinII domains.
claims.source: In particular, mossy fiber (Sotelo and Wassef, 1991; Voogd and Ruigrok, 1997; Ji and Hawkes, 1995; Armstrong et al., 2009) and CF (Voogd and Ruigrok, 1997; Chédotal et al., 1997; Sotelo and Chedotal, 2005) afferents terminate into parasagittal domains that align with the ZebrinII domains.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: CF development has been carefully described.
claims.source: CF development has been carefully described (Watanabe and Kano, 2011; Hashimoto et al., 2009; Kano et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: CF translocation occurs earlier in the nodular lobule X cerebellar region.
claims.source: Concomitantly with early maturation of the nodular lobule X described previously also CF translocation occurs earlier in this cerebellar region (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: The CS rate has never been found to be higher during development than in adulthood.
claims.source: Although PCs during development are innervated by multiple CFs (Hashimoto et al., 2009; Hashimoto and Kano, 2005), the CS rate has never been found to be higher during development than in adulthood (Arancillo et al., 2015; Sokoloff et al., 2015; Kawamura et al., 2013), and we verify that here for both Z+ and Z– populations.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and data from the current study.

claims.claim: CF pause duration is normalized after the period of synapse elimination at P18.
claims.source: Our data also reveal that CF pause duration is normalized after the period of synapse elimination at P18 (Figure 1D2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claims.claim: Initial dendritic outgrowth is known to be independent of input signals.
claims.source: Initial dendritic outgrowth is known to be independent of input signals (Sotelo and Arsenio-Nunes, 1976; Alvarado-Mallart and Sotelo, 1982; Dusart et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: CFs are necessary to complete PC dendritic growth and synapse maturation.
claims.source: However, CFs are necessary to complete PC dendritic growth and synapse maturation (Sotelo and Arsenio-Nunes, 1976; Sotelo, 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Positional cues from PCs are necessary for the correct CF-PC connection.
claims.source: Moreover, positional cues from PCs are necessary for the correct CF-PC connection (Chédotal et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: During the second postnatal week features substantial changes in PC axon arbors as well.
claims.source: During the second postnatal week features substantial changes in PC axon arbors as well.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data on axon arbor development.

claims.claim: Complexity and length of PC axon arbors both significantly increase between P7 and P10 and P14.
claims.source: Complexity and length both significantly increase between P7 and P10 and P14.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claims.claim: Between P14 and P21, morphological pruning appears to take place in PC axon arbors.
claims.source: However, between P14 and P21, morphological pruning appears to take place (Figure 5).

results.result: ZebrinII-related differences in simple spike (SS) firing rate emerge by P12 and persist into adulthood. Z− PCs exhibit significantly higher SS firing rates than Z+ PCs starting from P12-P17, with Z− PCs progressively increasing their firing rate until adulthood while Z+ PCs plateau at P18. SS regularity (CV2) does not differ between populations at P12-P17 but diverges from P18 onwards, with Z− PCs becoming more irregular than Z+ PCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37, C23, and C92 are supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings across multiple age groups (P12-P17, P18-P29, P30-P59, >P60) with appropriate statistical comparisons (p-values provided). The data show consistent developmental trajectories for both PC populations with clear statistical significance. Sample sizes appear adequate based on the scatter plots in figures, and the findings are internally consistent across related measures.

results.result: Complex spike (CS) activity and climbing fiber (CF) pause duration develop differentially between Z+ and Z− PCs. At P12-P17, Z+ PCs show significantly higher CS activity than Z− PCs, but this relationship reverses by P18-P27 and persists into adulthood. CF pause duration shows no difference at P12-P17 but becomes significantly longer in Z+ PCs compared to Z− PCs from P18 onwards, coinciding with the period of CF synapse elimination.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41, C95, and C105 are supported by in vivo recordings with statistical comparisons across developmental stages. The reversal in CS activity between P12-P17 and P18-P27 is clearly documented with p-values. The CF pause normalization after P18 aligns with known CF synapse elimination timing, providing biological plausibility. The data are internally consistent and appropriately analyzed.

results.result: Intrinsic firing rate differences between PC populations emerge at P12-P17 and are maintained into adulthood. In vitro recordings with synaptic blockers show that PC firing rates increase from P3-P5 to P10-P11 in both lobule III and X without regional differences. Starting at P12-P17, lobule X PCs exhibit significantly lower intrinsic firing rates than lobule III PCs, and this difference persists into adulthood. Irregularity (CV2) differences emerge from P18 onwards.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49, C24, C129-C130 are supported by in vitro cell-attached recordings with appropriate synaptic blockers (NMDA, AMPA, GABAA, glycine receptor antagonists) across seven age groups. The experimental design properly isolates intrinsic activity from synaptic inputs. Statistical comparisons are provided with p-values, and the developmental timeline is consistent with in vivo findings. The conclusion that differences are intrinsically driven (C49) is well-supported by the experimental approach.

results.result: Dendritic arborization develops differentially between anterior and nodular PC populations. From P6-P11 to P12-P17, all PCs show rapid increases in dendritic complexity and area. At P12-P17, there are no significant differences in dendritic complexity, maximum length, or area between lobules I-III and IX-X. However, from P18 onwards, lobules I-III PCs continue to grow significantly in complexity, length, and area into adulthood, while lobules IX-X PCs show only marginal changes after P12-P17.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54, C98-C99, and C138 are supported by Sholl analysis of biocytin-filled PCs across six age groups. The morphological data show clear developmental trajectories with statistical comparisons (p-values provided). The finding that dendritic differences emerge later (P18) than physiological differences (P12) is notable and well-documented. Sample sizes appear adequate based on scatter plots, and measurements are objective (intersections, length, area).

results.result: Climbing fiber (CF) translocation occurs earlier in nodular lobules compared to anterior lobules. At P7, lobules IX-X show significantly increased VGluT2 puncta and CF extension into the molecular layer compared to lobules I-III. From P7 to P14, molecular layer thickness increases dramatically in both regions and the differences in VGluT2 puncta and CF terminals disappear. From P21 into adulthood, molecular layer thickness becomes significantly greater in lobules I-III compared to lobules IX-X.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 and C103 are supported by immunohistochemical analysis of VGluT2 and calbindin staining across five age groups (P7, P14, P21, P35, P60). The quantification methods are clearly described (VGluT2 puncta density, CF height/ML height ratio, ML thickness measurements). Statistical comparisons show highly significant differences at P7 (p<0.0001) that disappear by P14, consistent with the interpretation of earlier CF translocation in nodular regions. Multiple measurements per image and multiple brains per age group provide adequate replication.

results.result: PC axon arbor development shows substantial changes during the second postnatal week with subtle differences between Z− and Z+ populations. Axon arbor complexity and length increase significantly from P7 to P14, then decrease at P21, while area continues to increase with age. Z− axon arbors exhibit denser branching complexity than Z+ arbors at P10, P14, and P21. Significant differences between Z− and Z+ groups are found for length and area but not number of intersections.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68, C109-C111, and C142 are supported by novel 3D Sholl analysis of sparsely labeled PC axon arbors in cerebellar nuclei using Pcp2-creERT2;Ai14 mice. The methodology is innovative and appropriate for studying axon development. Statistical comparisons are provided (p-values), and the finding of a peak at P14 followed by pruning is biologically plausible. The subtle differences between Z− and Z+ populations are appropriately characterized as such. Sample sizes appear adequate (at least 3 brains per age).

results.result: Baseline compensatory eye movements differ between juvenile (P21) and adult mice. OKR gain and phase do not differ significantly between age groups. However, VOR gain is significantly lower and VOR phase is significantly higher in juvenile mice compared to adults. VVOR phase shows no difference, but VVOR gain is significantly higher in juvenile animals compared to adults.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 and C146 are supported by compensatory eye movement recordings with appropriate controls and statistical comparisons. The experimental setup is well-described with proper calibration methods. The finding of lower VOR gain but similar OKR gain in juveniles is internally consistent and suggests delayed VOR maturation rather than general motor impairment. P-values are provided for all comparisons, and the data are presented clearly in supplementary figures.

results.result: Juvenile mice (P21-P25) show enhanced VOR phase reversal adaptation compared to adults. During 5 days of training, juvenile animals reverse their VOR phase faster with significantly lower gain values on the first 3 days and higher phase values on all days. Consolidation overnight is significantly larger in juvenile mice than adults for both gain decrease and phase increase. This suggests the flocculus circuitry at P21 is functional and may exhibit immature hyperplasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80, C28, C84, and C150 are supported by VOR phase reversal training data over 5 days with multiple training sessions per day. Statistical comparisons are provided (p-values for days 1-3 and consolidation measures). The experimental design properly controls for baseline differences and analyzes multiple aspects of learning (starting point, gaze, path/speed, consolidation). The interpretation of 'immature hyperplasticity' is appropriately cautious and supported by citations to similar developmental phenomena in other systems.

results.result: Juvenile mice (P21) show attenuated eyeblink conditioning (EBC) compared to adults. Juvenile animals exhibit significantly lower conditioned response (CR) percentage after the first day of learning and reduced amplitude of eyelid closure in response to the conditioned stimulus. This difference is not due to reduced eyelid closure abilities, as unconditioned response (UR) timing and onset are similar between age groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83, C30, and C84 are supported by EBC behavioral data with appropriate controls. The experimental design includes proper analysis of both conditioned and unconditioned responses, ruling out motor impairments as an explanation. Statistical comparisons are provided (p=0.027 for CR percentage). The use of a visual cue (LED) rather than auditory cue addresses potential confounds from immature sensory pathways. Sample sizes and methods are clearly described.

results.result: Different PC subpopulations acquire unique morphological and physiological features during distinct developmental timelines, with nodular/Z+ PCs reaching adult stages earlier than anterior/Z− PCs. All PCs show rapid development in the second postnatal week, but anterior PCs have prolonged physiological and dendritic maturation. These differential developmental timelines match with region-specific cerebellar behaviors: younger mice show attenuated anterior-dependent eyeblink conditioning but faster nodular-dependent compensatory eye movement adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C8, C32, C85-C86, C90, C145, C164, and C170 represent the main conclusions integrating physiological, morphological, and behavioral data. The evidence is comprehensive and internally consistent across multiple experimental approaches (in vivo recordings, in vitro recordings, morphological analysis, immunohistochemistry, behavioral testing). The correlation between cellular maturation timelines and behavioral performance is compelling, though causality is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The conclusion is appropriately cautious and well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental modalities.

results.result: The influence of extrinsic inputs on PC firing develops differentially between regions. Extrinsic inputs (net effect of excitatory and inhibitory inputs) have relatively small influence in the second postnatal week but begin driving activity at P18. This influence remains relatively stable in nodular lobule X/Z+ PCs but increases over time for anterior lobule III/Z− PCs until full maturation in adults.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C133 and C96 are supported by comparison of in vivo and in vitro firing rates across developmental stages. The delta between in vivo and in vitro rates provides a reasonable estimate of input-driven activity, though this approach cannot distinguish between individual input types or changes in excitation/inhibition balance. The interpretation is appropriately cautious, and the data are presented clearly in supplementary figures. The finding complements the intrinsic activity data and provides additional insight into circuit maturation.

results.result: Interpretive claims suggest that PC configuration follows from birthdate-determined development, maturation is coupled to physiological development, axon arbor differences are set early, and reduced firing rates in young anterior PCs may contribute to impaired eyeblink conditioning through limitations in intrinsic excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C91, C100, C115, C153, C162, and C163 represent inferences and speculations beyond the direct data. While these interpretations are reasonable given the evidence, they involve mechanistic claims (e.g., birthdate determining configuration, excitability limitations explaining behavior) that are not directly tested. C162 and C163 are explicitly speculative. These claims would benefit from additional experiments directly testing the proposed mechanisms, such as birthdate labeling studies or manipulation of intrinsic excitability in young animals.
